although systems like ArrayG can enhance signal brightness and tracking duration,
they often interfere with native protein mobility with significantly reduced diffusion
coefficients (~0.14 µm²/s). Moreover, ReTag8’s reversible fluorogenic labeling
maintained a constant number of trajectories (>80%) for over 5 minutes of continuous
observation without any wash or exchange steps, whereas fewer than 20% of Halo-Tag-
labeled proteins remained visible under the same conditions (new added Fig. 6n and
S40b).
These new results highlight that ReTag8 provides superior brightness for protein
labeling with minimal interference to protein mobility. The new data and discussion
have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (line 470) and Supplementary
Figure 40.
10. The study claims that ReTagX’s small size minimizes interference with protein
function. However, functional assays are needed to confirm that tagged proteins retain
their biological activity. Given the significant brightness enhancement of ReTag8,
its potential impact on protein diffusion and cellular function should also be examined.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important and constructive
suggestion. We fully agree that ensuring the functional compatibility of tagged proteins
is essential, especially for array systems. While ReTag4 (~78 kD) and ReTag8 (~156
kD) is indeed larger than commonly used tags such as GFP or HaloTag, it remains
significantly smaller than existing array systems (e.g., SunTag, ArrayG; >1 MDa),
which are known to perturb protein dynamics (Nat. Chem. Biol. 2019, 15, 401).
To support the biocompatibility of ReTagX, we have fused ReTag 1 and ReTag4 to
several representative proteins across cellular compartments, e.g. H2B (nucleus),
TOM20 and MitoNEET (mitochondria), and vimentin (cytoskeleton), and confirmed
correct subcellular localization without observable disruption to protein function or
cellular phenotype (Fig. 4-5 and Fig. 6a-d). To further evaluate the impact on protein
dynamics, we tested ReTag8 in the context of TNFR2, a membrane protein with well-
characterized diffusion behavior. Compared to TNFR2-HaloTag, TNFR2-ReTag8
showed a 5.5-fold increase in brightness (Fig. 6i). Importantly, single-molecule tracking
revealed a diffusion coefficient of 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s for TNFR2–ReTag8, closely
matching the reported value of 0.30 ± 0.028 µm²/s for TNFR2–HaloTag (Fig. 6m–n;
Fig. S40), indicating minimal perturbation to mobility. This contrasts with existing
multivalent tags such as ArrayG, which—despite increased brightness—have been
shown to significantly impair protein diffusion (~0.14 µm²/s) due to their large size.
Together, these results suggest that ReTagX achieves substantial brightness
enhancement while minimizing disruption to protein dynamics and cellular function.
We have revised the manuscript and Supplementary Figure S40 to incorporate this
discussion (line 470).
11. The fluorescence enhancement of ReTag8 (~5.2×) is promising, but its potential for
Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) or other photophysical interactions is not
addressed. Could the close spatial arrangement of fluorophores cause quenching or
spectral crosstalk? This could affect quantitative fluorescence measurements.
Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) should be performed to assess
potential FRET effects. Additionally, testing the linearity of fluorescence intensity
relative to fluorophore number would confirm accurate single-molecule quantification.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree
that labeling with multiple dyes can potentially lead to self-quenching via mechanisms
such as homo-FRET, particularly when fluorophores are spaced within <10 nm (Chem
Soc Rev, 2020, 49, 5110). We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to use FLIM to
evaluate potential FRET effects; however, this measurement is currently limited by the
lack of available instrumentation in our facility. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that
previous studies using systems like SunTag, ArrayG, and fluorescent light-up aptamers
(FLAPs) have shown that introducing multiple dyes at sub-10 nm distances can
achieve >10-fold brightness enhancement without significant quenching. This is
probably because self-quenching depends not only on distance but also on the dipole
orientation of fluorophores (Phys. Chem. B 1999, 103, 6839; J. Biophotonics. 2018, 11,
e201700366.). In our study, ReTag1, ReTag2, and ReTag4 exhibited a linear increase
in fluorescence intensity (Fig. S36). Furthermore, single-molecule imaging of purified
ReTag4 immobilized on glass revealed discrete stepwise intensity increments,
consistent with minimal quenching effects (Fig. 6i). Additionally, ReTag8 fusions
exhibited a 5.5-fold increase in brightness at the single-protein level compared to the
widely used Halo-Tag, although we cannot fully exclude the possibility of quenching
due to FRET effects.
We agree with reviewer that precise stoichiometric quantification remains
challenging due to the reversible labeling of ReTagX and potential quenching. However,
it is worth noting that we mainly focus on the increased brightness and long-term
imaging due to the unique fluorogenic and reversible binding property. A discussion of
potential FRET effects and their implications has been added to the revised manuscript
(Line 544-546) and supplementary file (Fig. S36).
12. Some figures (e.g., Fig. 3i) lack statistical analysis or error bars, making it difficult
to assess reproducibility; the Fig. 2 appears oversaturated, which is not conducive to
observing image details.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In Fig. 3i, the error bars were
previously displayed using a light color, which may have made them difficult to
distinguish. We have now recolored them in the revised Fig. 3j to improve visibility and
facilitate assessment of data reproducibility.
The images in Fig. 2 were acquired under standard imaging conditions. The
apparent oversaturation resulted from post-acquisition brightness enhancement in
ImageJ, which was applied uniformly across the image to better visualize low
background signals in the cytosol. Importantly, no nonspecific labeling or signal
aggregation was observed, even after increasing brightness. To address the reviewer’s
concern and ensure transparency, we have now included the original, unprocessed
images in the revised Supplementary Information (Fig. S4, S5 and S9) for direct
comparison and clearer assessment of image details and background.
13. The distinction between different fluorogenic ligands in figures should be clearer,
such as through color-coding.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion to improve clarity. In the
revised figures, the different fluorogenic ligands have been redrawn with clearer
distinction. Key structural differences, such as O, C(CH₃)₂, and Si(CH₃)₂, are now color-
coded to make them easier to differentiate and improve overall readability.
14. From the Figure S10, we can see that the cell positions in the second to fourth
images are consistent. Why did the position of the cell image change after a time
interval of 1 hour, and the signal became stronger at an interval of 4 hours? The light
radiation experiment results at different positions are not convincing, and it is
unreasonable that the signal does not weaken but becomes stronger after 4 hours
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The cell imaging
shown in Figure S10 was performed in fixed cells. Due to limited instrument
availability and scheduling constraints, we imaged different cells at each time point
rather than repeatedly imaging the same cell over the 4-hour period. Additionally, some
cells appeared brighter, likely due to variability in expression levels. To minimize the
influence of expression variability of different cells on fluorescence quantification, we
have co-expressed ReTag with SNAP-Tag and stained the cells with SiR-BG (shown in
red) as an internal control. In the revised manuscript, we present the normalized
fluorescence ratio, which demonstrates that the signal remains stable even after 4 hours.
The relatively stable fluorescence signal from TMP-Tag is likely due to a
conformational change that forms a closed state in the presence of NADPH and TMP
derivatives, resulting in extremely high binding affinity (~pM) and slow release kinetics
(Biochim. Biophys. Acta, 1994, 1207, 74; Structure, 2009, 17, 386). This mechanism
helps maintain signal stability over extended periods, as reflected in our new
quantification data included in the revised Supplementary file (Fig. S12). We have
added this explanation to the revised manuscript (Line 256).
15. The ReTag1 probe does show good anti-bleaching properties in STED super-
resolution imaging, but the resolution improvement is not very obvious (Figure 4). The
author should measure the saturated stimulated emission power of the ReTag1 probe
and compare it with the commercial probe ATTO647.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In response,
we have repeated the STED images in Fig. 4a by applying stronger laser power (~219
mW) to improve image quality. With this optimized approach, we achieved a full width
at half maximum (FWHM) of 43 ± 5 nm for vimentin filaments in live cells under wash-
free STED conditions, representing the leading enhanced spatial resolution and imaging
quality compared with reported work (Nat Commun, 2022, 13, 2264; J. Am. Chem. Soc.
2023, 145, 3075). In this work, we intentionally avoided using saturated STED power
to minimize photobleaching and enable longer-term imaging at nanoscale resolution (~
80 nm) from 5 frames to 300 frames, which is a key advantage of our system.
As ATTO647, due to its hydrophilic structure, is not suitable for live-cell
applications, we instead compared MaP655-TMP with SiR-Halo, a widely used
commercial STED probe compatible with live-cell imaging (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2019,
141, 7, 2770). As shown in the revised Fig. 4b and S26, under wash-free conditions,
SiR-Halo exhibited poor resolution, rapid photobleaching, and high background, with
signal typically detectable for only 1–5 frames. In contrast, ReTag1 labeled with
MaP655-TMP enabled improved spatial resolution (FWHM: 43–80 nm) and sustained
high-contrast imaging for 15-300 frames under wash-free conditions. We have added
new data in the revised supplementary file (Fig. S26).
16. Although the authors mentioned the toxicity of the probe in the conclusion, they did
not provide a cell toxicity experiment. It is recommended that the authors add a cell
toxicity experiment.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we
conducted a cytotoxicity evaluation using the CCK-8 assay. As shown in Fig. S10,
U2OS cells incubated with the probe at 2 μM and 10 μM for 12 and 24 hours exhibited
no significant reduction in cell viability, indicating negligible cytotoxicity under the
tested conditions. These results confirm that the fluorogenic probe is highly
biocompatible and suitable for live-cell applications. The new data have been added in
the revised supplementary file (Fig. S10).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
1. In their work “A Bright and Regenerative Array Tag with Fluorogenic Ligands for
Long-Term Live-Cell Nanoscopy and Single Molecule Tracking,” Si et al. investigate
the potential of their newly developed ReTag system, which is based on a mutagenized
TMP-tag system in combination with fluorogenic ligands. Unlike the commonly used
SNAPtag or HaloTag, this TMP system has the advantage of being noncovalent from
the outset. Newly tested mutations decreased the binding duration of the labeled protein
while maintaining the high association rates of the TMP-tag. Combined with its small
size, this system could represent a significant advancement in transient protein labeling,
especially when used alongside more established systems for multi color approaches.
The authors emphasize their ambition for the ReTag system across various modern
microscopy techniques, which pose demanding requirements for any fluorescent protein
or dye. I am excited about every new protein labeling system, especially when it allows
for efficient intracellular fluorescent labeling in combination with transient binding.
However, before I can fully recommend accepting this manuscript, I have some
lingering questions, comments, and recommendations for experimental additions:
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and encouraging
summary of our work. We truly appreciate the reviewer’s enthusiasm for new protein
labeling systems and their constructive comments. In response, we have conducted
additional experiments, cell viability under MaP655-TMP labeling (Fig. S10),
comparison of fluorescence self-recovery among ReTag1, ReTag4, and XHaloTag (Fig.
S25), effects of STED laser illumination on cellular Ca²⁺ and ROS levels (Fig. S29 and
S30), wash-free STED nanoscopy of vimentin filaments (Fig. 4a), brightness
comparison between ReTag4 and ReTag8 (Fig. S38), detailed single-molecule tracking
of TNFR2 (e.g. brightness, diffusion, and duration) (Fig. 6k-o, Fig. S39-40). We have
also expanded our discussion to improve clarity on points as suggested. We believe that
the revised manuscript has been substantially strengthened thanks to the reviewer’s
insightful recommendations.
2. Perhaps I'm missing something, but the values in Figure 3e don't make any sense to
me. The dissociation constant (KD) should simply be koff/kon, yet this does not appear
to be reflected in the table.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The KD values presented
in Figure 3e were determined through steady-state binding analysis using the Sartorius
Octet R8 system, a widely used instrument for measuring binding affinities. In this
method, equilibrium responses (Req) at various analyte concentrations are fit to a 1:1
Langmuir binding isotherm using the following equation:
𝑅𝑚𝑎𝑥 ×[𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐.]
𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒 =
𝐾D+[𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐.]
where Response is the equilibrium binding signal, Rmax is the maximum binding
capacity, [Conc.] is the analyte concentration, and KD is the equilibrium dissociation
constant.
This steady-state model allows for direct extraction of KD from equilibrium
binding levels across multiple concentrations, independent of the kinetic parameters
kon and koff. As such, the KD values reported in Figure 3e are derived from equilibrium
isotherms and not calculated from k /k . To prevent further confusion, we have now
off on
clarified this KD derivation method in the Methods section and added a corresponding
note in the figure legend.
3. Could the authors comment on why they chose to conduct FRAP experiments in live
cells (Fig. 3i), especially considering they demonstrated in Figure 3f that it is possible
to stain the same construct in fixed cells? While H2B's diffusion is slow, shouldn't there
be concerns about how this might impact the results?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and important comment. We chose
to conduct FRAP experiments in live cells because the primary goal of our study is to
establish a reversible labeling platform that functions robustly under live-cell imaging
conditions, where labeling kinetics, probe concentration, environmental variability, and
cellular toxicity are critical considerations.
As the reviewer correctly notes, histone H2B is a slow-diffusing nuclear protein,
making it a suitable model for evaluating fluorescence recovery driven by probe
exchange without significant interference from protein mobility. To further ensure that
the observed recovery is due to probe dynamics rather than protein diffusion, we
included controls using irreversible labeling systems such as SNAP-Tag with SiR-BG
and eDHFR-tag with TMP-based probes, which showed minimal fluorescence recovery
under identical imaging conditions. These results highlight that the robust recovery
observed with ReTag is indeed due to its dynamic and reversible labeling mechanism,
not from H2B mobility. We have clarified this rationale and added appropriate
discussion in the revised manuscript (Line 295 and 300).
4. In lines 338 to 344, the authors present their first STED experiments using Vimentin-
ReTag1-Halo and claim that this system, labeled with MaP655-TMP, outperforms the
conventional HaloTag, producing 15 consecutive super-resolution images compared to
one image with poor resolution obtained using the HaloTag under the same conditions.
However, Figure S23, which is referenced as evidence, mentions Tom20-Halo on the
left side, not Vimentin. Furthermore, while I do not doubt that the ReTag outperforms
the standard HaloTag in long-term STED experiments, I find it hard to believe that a
combination of a commonly used tag for STED, paired with one of the most widely used
dyes for STED, would fail to yield even a single STED image with good resolution.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the careful observation and for pointing
out the labeling error in Figure S23. The images originally labeled as Tom20-Halo
actually depict vimentin structures. We have now corrected the figure labeling and
reorganized the panel accordingly to avoid confusion. As shown in the previous
supplementary file (Fig. S23), SiR-Halo performs poorly under wash-free STED
conditions. This limitation likely arises from residual unbound fluorophores at the 200
nM concentration, which contribute to elevated background fluorescence under high
depletion laser power; therefore, washing steps are usually required in STED
nanoscopy (Nat. Chem. 2013, 5, 132).
To further compare the performance between Halo-Tag and ReTag1, we repeated
the STED experiments with SiR-Halo under optimized conditions, including a thorough
washing step after probe incubation. As shown in revised Fig. S26, even under these
optimized conditions, Vimentin-Halo labeled with SiR-Halo sustained only less than 5
frames of STED imaging due to rapid photobleaching. In contrast, Vimentin-ReTag1
labeled with MaP655-TMP achieved 10-15 consecutive super-resolution frames,
owing to the exchangeable and fluorogenic nature of the ReTag system, which
minimizes background signal and enables longer imaging durations under the same
laser conditions. We have updated the figure, corrected the labeling, and added this
discussion to the revised manuscript (Line 354) and supplementary file (Fig. S26).
5. In lines 355 to 359, the authors assert that they can track mitochondria with a
resolution of 80 nm over 100 minutes or more than 300 frames. However, upon
reviewing Movie 1, which is intended to showcase this “unprecedented achievement,”
I found it somewhat confusing. The movie cuts off after 50 minutes without any
explanation, and it is only mentioned in the supplementary material that the cell had to
be refocused after several time points. Does this not imply that the exposure was also
reduced during those intervals? Furthermore, the entire sample appeared to drift out
of the region of interest (ROI), resulting in only a small fraction of the mitochondria
being illuminated between approximately 30 and 41 minutes. However, this sample drift
is not evident in the figure. Additionally, there is a significant jump in frames shown in
the figure between frames 130 to 200 and frame 270, indicating a different interval than
previously used. Based on the appearance of the mitochondria after 270 frames, the
cell appeared stressed due to phototoxicity and likely dying, yet this observation was
not mentioned by the authors.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful assessment and insightful comments
regarding the long-term STED imaging experiment presented in Movie 1. As this
experiment involves continuous imaging of living cells for over 100 minutes, cellular
movement and mitochondrial repositioning are indeed unavoidable. During imaging,
we observed mitochondrial migration away from the field of view, likely in response to
photostimulation. To maintain consistent tracking of the same mitochondria, the
imaging position was realigned at 17, 42, and 60 minutes, with each adjustment
requiring approximately 5 seconds. A distinctive circular mitochondrion, marked with
a white arrow, was used as a positional reference to ensure continuity.
As the reviewer rightly noted, continuous imaging under STED laser can induce
phototoxicity (Nat. Methods, 2018, 15, 755). Meanwhile, some degree of photodamage
may also result from the suboptimal live-cell conditions, as the STEDYCON system
used in this study is limited to imaging buffer and does not support full cell culture
conditions (e.g. controlled temperature, CO₂, and humidity). In addition, we conducted
additional experiments (Fig. S30) assessing reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels under
prolonged STED exposure. These results confirm that continuous STED illumination
increases ROS levels, particularly in fluorescent labeled cells. While this ROS elevation
did not cause overt cell death during the imaging period, it may have induced cellular
stress, leading to changes in mitochondrial morphology.
We have now discussed this limitation more explicitly in the revised manuscript and
included recommendations for minimizing phototoxicity in future studies, such as the
use of ROS scavengers (Nat. Methods, 2018, 15, 755), improved imaging platforms
(e.g., Abberior Facility STED), and optimized cell culture conditions. We have updated
the main text and figure legend (Lines 373-381 and S28). In addition, we have included
time-lapse STED images of live U2OS cells, shown at 20-frame intervals in Fig. S28
of revised supplementary file.
6. Regarding the authors' tracking experiments, I have several questions: There is no
comparison to other more commonly used intracellular tagging systems, such as the
HaloTag, SNAPtag, or even the reHaloTag and xHTL labeling systems. This absence
makes it difficult to assess the acquired results effectively.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To benchmark ReTagX
against established intracellular labeling systems, we directly compared it with the
widely used Halo-Tag under identical imaging conditions. A single ReTag8 molecule
exhibited a 5.5-fold higher brightness than Halo-Tag-labeled proteins. After extended
time-lapse acquisition, a constant number of TNFR2-ReTag8 trajectories (>80%)
remained detectable over 5 minutes, whereas fewer than 20% of Halo-Tag-labeled
trajectories persisted beyond 1 minute, indicating a significantly extended observation
window for ReTag8. Furthermore, track-frame distribution analysis revealed that
ReTag8 enabled a 2.9-fold longer average tracking duration compared to Halo-Tag.
Importantly, the measured diffusion coefficient of TNFR2-ReTag8 was
0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s, closely matching the reported value of ~0.30 µm²/s (Biochim.
Biophys. Acta, 2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40), suggesting that ReTag8 does
not significantly perturb protein mobility.
These results demonstrate that ReTagX offers substantially enhanced brightness,
prolonged tracking duration, and minimal impact on protein dynamics, thereby
providing significant advantages over conventional Halo-Tag for single-molecule
imaging in live cells. The new data and discussion were added in the revised manuscript
(Line 470-483, Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40)
7. As stated, imaging was conducted with 30% laser intensity and 200 ms exposure for
brightness evaluation, and with 10% laser intensity and 50 ms exposure for
fluorescence lifetime (this term is normally used in another context). These values lack
context. The authors should include measured power densities or power at the back
focal plane. Additionally, they should provide a range of power densities for the actual
tracking experiments; currently, it's only noted as "set to optimize signal-to-noise."
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion to improve the clarity and
reproducibility of our imaging conditions. As requested, we have measured and
included the laser power densities used during single-molecule imaging. We fused
TNFR2 with Halo-Tag labeled with SiR-Halo (1 nM) and ReTag8 labeled with
MaP655-TMP (200 nM). In vitro single-molecule imaging with 640 nm laser
illumination was performed at the following measured intensities: 30% (30.4 W/cm²),
60% (60.4 W/cm²), and 100% (99.1 W/cm²). We used 60% laser intensity (60.4 W/cm²),
which provided an optimal balance between signal-to-noise ratio and photobleach
(newly added Fig. S39).
Representative images acquired under varying illumination powers have been
included in the revised Supplementary Information (Fig. S39). Additionally, the term
“fluorescence lifetime” has been revised to avoid potential misunderstanding.
8. Fusing multiple ReTags into an array is a good idea in principle, but it contradicts
the general aim of having a small tag that does not hinder diffusion. Once the authors
added the second ReTag, the size of their system became larger than that of the HaloTag
(36 kDa compared to 33 kDa). What is the advantage here?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that
the development of array tags inherently increases the overall molecular size, which
can potentially influence protein function and mobility. For instance, the Array G
system (~1.0 MDa) has been shown to markedly reduce the mobility of membrane
protein β1 from 0.25 to 0.14 µm²/s (Nat. Chem. Biol., 2019, 15, 401). However, such
strategies also offer distinct advantages, particularly in enhancing fluorescence
brightness and extending imaging duration (Cell, 2014, 159, 635; Nat. Chem. Biol.,
2019, 15, 401).
In this work, ReTag8 (~156 kDa) provides a 5.5-fold increase in brightness per
protein compared to Halo-Tag (~36 kDa). Moreover, the exchangeable binding of
ReTag8 allows sustained fluorescence signals even as individual fluorophores bleach,
resulting in approximately a 2.9-fold longer single-molecule tracking duration and
significantly extended observation windows (>5 min) (Fig. 6) compared to monovalent
tags like Halo-Tag (<1 min). Notably, the measured diffusion coefficient of TNFR2-
ReTag8 was 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s, closely matching the reported value of ~0.30 µm²/s
(Biochim. Biophys. Acta, 2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40), suggesting minimal
impact on protein mobility.
Taken together, these results highlight that ReTagX provides a rational compromise
between tag size and imaging performance. It offers a modular, tunable platform with
enhanced brightness and photostability, while maintaining biological compatibility. We
are actively working to develop smaller, high-performance ReTag variants to further
minimize potential cellular perturbations. This discussion has been incorporated into
the revised manuscript (lines 541-546).
9. In this context, diffusion coefficients or mean square displacements were never
measured in any of the experiments.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To directly
address the concern, we performed single-molecule imaging to evaluate whether
ReTagX affects protein diffusion. Specifically, we fused ReTag8 to Tumor Necrosis
Factor Receptor 2 (TNFR2) for single-molecule tracking in live U2OS cells. As
presented in the revised manuscript, we quantified the diffusion coefficient of TNFR2-
ReTag8 and obtained a value of 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s. This is in close agreement with the
previously reported diffusion coefficient of ~0.30 µm²/s for TNFR2 (Biochim. Biophys.
Acta, 2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40). These results indicate that ReTag8 does
not significantly alter the native mobility of membrane proteins, supporting its
suitability for minimally perturbative, long-term imaging. We have now included these
data and the corresponding analysis in the revised manuscript (line 470-483, Fig. 6k-
6o) and Supplementary Information (Fig. S40).
10. No software is mentioned for the tracking analysis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The software “Python” used for
tracking analysis has been added to the revised Image Data Analysis section of the
Supplementary Information (line 1200-1203).
11. CAAX or other farnesylated proteins tend to diffuse quite rapidly, especially at 37 °C.
The motion blur present at the reported 20 Hz acquisition speed may hinder tracking
fidelity. I recommend repeating the experiments with a faster exposure time to improve
the results.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To minimize motion
blur and enhance tracking fidelity for ReTagX, we fused ReTag8 with a membrane
receptor Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor 2 (TNFR2) and performed single-molecule
tracking at an increased frame rate using a reduced exposure time of 30 ms (~33 Hz).
As shown in the revised manuscript, the measured diffusion coefficient of TNFR2–
ReTag8 was 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s, closely matching the previously reported value of
~0.30 µm²/s (Biochim. Biophys. Acta, 2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40). These
results demonstrate that ReTag8 supports high-fidelity tracking without significantly
perturbing the native mobility of membrane proteins, underscoring its utility for
minimally invasive, long-term imaging applications. We have now included these data
and the corresponding analysis in the revised manuscript (line 470, Fig. 6k-6o) and
Supplementary Information (Fig. S40).
12. The increase in tracking duration appears to stem mainly from the ability to reduce
laser power due to the enhanced brightness of multiple bound MaP-TMP ligand. At
least, this is what can be inferred from reading the manuscript. I strongly recommend
comparing ReTag8 to an 8xTMP-tag to demonstrate that the improved performance is
due to rebinding. Additionally, please ensure that the same laser power is used for both
experiments.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In ReTag8, the more
than 5-fold increased brightness is a major advantage that allows us to track single
proteins using lower laser power. We agree with the reviewer that reduced laser power
for ReTag8 can contribute to prolonged tracking time.
As the reviewer required, we conducted a comparison between TNFR2 labeled with
ReTag8 and with an 8×TMP-Tag construct under identical imaging conditions,
especially with same laser power. Interestingly, we observed that the mean tracking
duration of TNFR2-ReTag8 was approximately 2.8-fold longer than that of TNFR2-
TMP-Tag8. Moreover, a constant number of TNFR2-ReTag8 trajectories (>80%)
remained detectable after 5 minutes of imaging, whereas fewer than 20% of TMP-Tag8
trajectories persisted beyond 1 minute (new added Fig. 6n and Fig. S40). These results
suggest that reversible binding plays a key role in prolonging signal longevity during single-
molecule tracking.
We acknowledge that the improvement in tracking duration between ReTag8 and
TMP-Tag8 is modest and warrants optimization in future work, particularly of the
binding and dissociation kinetics, to extend residence time and enable efficient
exchange upon photobleaching. In parallel, we are working to engineer smaller ReTag
variants to support higher-order assemblies while minimizing tag size. This comparison
and the associated discussion have been added to the revised manuscript (line 541, Fig.
6n and S40).
13. Transiently binding probes show their greatest strengths in prolonged imaging
experiments lasting minutes or even hours. The authors choose to label CAAX proteins
after a very short expression time point, when only a few proteins are present inside the
cell. The standard practice would be to wait for higher expression levels and label only
a subfraction of all CAAX proteins. Following this, one could conduct prolonged
imaging to demonstrate that, with the same ligand concentrations, ReTag8 outperforms
the TMP-tag or even the 8xTMP-tag, with a much milder decrease in the number of
localizations over time. This approach has been successfully employed with xHTL dyes
and the reHaloTag, for example. I highly recommend that the authors conduct this
experiment.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive
suggestion. We fully agree that transiently binding probes show their greatest utility in
prolonged imaging under more physiological expression levels, as elegantly
demonstrated in the work of Prof. Mike Heilemann and colleagues with exchangeable
HaloTag systems (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202413117). In those studies,
membrane proteins were allowed to express at higher levels (~ 1d), and sub-
stoichiometric labeling with fluorogenic dyes (e.g., SiR-S5, JF585-Hy4) enabled
efficient single-molecule tracking with low background and minimal perturbation.
Taking inspiration from this approach, we conducted additional experiments
where cells were transfected for 6 h and then allowed to express the TNFR2-ReTag8
overnight (~12 h) before imaging. In single molecule imaging, we observed a markedly
slower decrease in localization density over time as the reviewer assumed. Specifically,
a constant number of TNFR2-ReTag8 trajectories (>80%) remained detectable after 5
minutes of imaging, whereas fewer than 20% of TMP-Tag8 and Halo-Tag-SiR
trajectories persisted beyond 1 minute under identical conditions. These results suggest
that the dynamic and reversible nature of the ReTag system contributes to more
sustained signal retention. We have included these new data and discussions in the
revised manuscript (line 470, Fig. 6m-6o).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
1. This paper describes a bright and regenerative tag system (ReTag) and highly
fluorogenic ligands that provide bright labeling with minimal background. The authors
show how this tag allows greatly extended STED imaging or time-lapse SIM imaging
of mitochondrial TOM20, revealing mitochondrial dynamics such as fission, fusion,
and elongation. STED, multi-color SIM and MINFLUX images of Vimentin-ReTag1 all
show impressive resolution. In addition, the compact ReTag8 array tag fused to CAAX
is used as an example of tracking a membrane protein in living cells, which extends
imaging duration by ~4-fold (up to 10 seconds) compared to the conventional TMP-
Tag.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their positive summary and
encouraging evaluation of our work.
2. The images generated with the ReTag are impressive, so this tag and the ligands will
be useful to the field. However, the paper is very dense, especially the first half, with 22
supplementary figures described along with only 3 main figures. It is difficult to
navigate the first half of the results section as the many supplementary figures are
typically very poorly described, e.g. lines 251 and 253 show single sentence descriptions
of Figs S9 and S10. It would help the reader to explain the supplementary data properly
in the text and give more information in the legend. For me, Fig. S9 needs more explanation.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their positive remarks on the image
quality and for recognizing the potential utility of the ReTag system and ligands for the
field. As the reviewer required, we have carefully revised the manuscript to improve
clarity and readability. Specifically, we have expanded the descriptions of
supplementary figures within the main text to provide more context and explanation
(see revised line 181 for S4 and S5; line 217 for S7; lines 252-258 for S11 and S12; line
306 for S24 and S25). Additionally, considering the limited context provided in the
main manuscript, we have substantially updated the legends of the supplementary
figures to give more detailed information on the experimental conditions, results, and
their relevance to the main findings. These improvements will make the manuscript
easier to navigate and help readers better appreciate the supporting data.
3. My major concern relates to the idea that multimerization of ReTag could be a
potential alternative to e.g. the SunTag array, which would be advantageous based on
the smaller size of ReTag4/8. As the SunTag is primarily used for imaging translation,
ideally translation would be imaged with ReTag4/8. However, my bigger concern
relates to the idea that ReTag8 can be used to quantitate fluorescence as a proxy for
e.g. translation when there is reversible exchange of bleached fluorophores. As far as I
understand it, quantitation of translation using SunTag relies on stable binding of scFv
so that, after correcting for bleaching, the changes in fluorescence can be directly
attributed to changes in ribosome density. If ReTag8 is used and there is bleaching, then
exchange of bleached fluorophores, how can variations in signal due to this exchange
be separated from changes in e.g. ribosome density?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and important comment.
We fully agree that the SunTag system, with its stable and irreversible binding of scFv,
is ideally suited for quantifying translation by correlating fluorescence intensity with
ribosome density after correcting for photobleaching. Indeed, due to its fast ligand
exchange, ReTag8 is not intended to replace SunTag for translation quantification.
Rather, our goal with ReTag8 is to address different limitations, primarily those related
to tag size, photobleaching, and brightness in live-cell single-molecule imaging.
Specifically, the smaller size of individual ReTag units enables construction of
multivalent arrays with reduced steric hindrance compared to large systems like SunTag
or ArrayG (>1 MDa), which have been reported to perturb protein mobility.
To explore the performance of ReTag8 in this context, we fused it to the
transmembrane protein TNFR2 and performed single-molecule tracking in live U2OS
cells. Compared with TNFR2-Halo-Tag, TNFR2-ReTag8 showed a 5.5-fold increase in
brightness and enabled longer-term tracking (Fig. 6i). Importantly, the measured
diffusion coefficient of TNFR2-ReTag8 was 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s, closely matching the
known diffusion coefficient of ~0.30 µm²/s for this receptor (Biochim. Biophys. Acta,
2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40), suggesting that ReTag8 does not significantly
interfere with protein dynamics. In contrast, large tag arrays like ArrayG have been
shown to reduce mobility considerably (e.g., to 0.14 µm²/s) (Nat. Chem. Biol., 2019,
15, 401), which may limit their applicability for studying dynamic membrane or
cytoplasmic proteins.
In summary, while ReTag8 is not ideal for quantitative translation imaging due to
its exchangeable binding, it offers key advantages for minimally perturbative, extended-duration single-molecule imaging. We have clarified this distinction and
added relevant discussion in the revised manuscript (line 476 and line 544, Fig. 6m-60,
and S40).
4. In addition, it is described how ReTag8 extends the imaging time to ~10 seconds in
living cells, but typical SunTag imaging durations are >30 mins for translation.
Therefore, it is unclear to what extent multimerising ReTag will be useful as an
alternative array, other than for short-term bright imaging. If the authors only mean
ReTag4/8 is better than the conventional TMP-Tag, it would be better not to mention
SunTag.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and important comment.
SunTag system is well established for long-term translation imaging, with reported
durations exceeding 30 minutes. Such experiments are typically performed with
relatively long acquisition intervals and exposure times (e.g., 20-500 ms), resulting in
lower imaging frequencies (~1 Hz) (Nat. Protoco., 2020, 15, 1371)
In contrast, our study focused on fast single-molecule imaging under higher
temporal resolution (33 Hz), where fluorophore exchange and photobleaching present
different challenges. Under these conditions, we observed that ReTag8 supports single-
molecule tracking durations of 1-10 seconds, which is in a comparable range to other
systems used for high-speed acquisition—for example, ~1.9 s at 5 Hz for kinesin-1 with
SunTag, ~34 s at 20 Hz for integrin β1 with ArrayG, and ~1.6 s at 33 Hz for H2B with
HA-tag (Table S1). These comparisons suggest that multimeric ReTag constructs can
perform competitively under fast imaging regimes, particularly for tracking highly
dynamic targets. Moreover, we found that ReTag8 does not noticeably perturb the
mobility of the fused protein. Specifically, TNFR2-ReTag8 exhibited a diffusion
coefficient of 0.28 ± 0.019 µm²/s, closely matching the literature value of ~0.30 µm²/s
for this receptor (Biochim. Biophys. Acta, 2010, 1798, 1081) (Fig. 6m-n; Fig. S40). This
suggests that ReTag8 is minimally invasive in terms of molecular dynamics. In contrast,
larger arrays such as ArrayG, while offering long observation times, have been reported
to reduce mobility significantly (e.g., to ~0.14 µm²/s), potentially limiting their
application in certain contexts.
Thus, we agree with the reviewer that direct comparisons to SunTag in the context
of translation imaging may lead to confusion, as ReTag8 currently lacks the stable
binding necessary for quantitative translation assays. We have therefore revised the
manuscript to clarify the intended application scope of ReTag8 and have adjusted the
discussion to focus on its advantages in single-molecule tracking, rather than long-term
translation monitoring. We have incorporated these clarifications into the revised
manuscript (line 550).
Minor comments
5. The first Results section on the design seems a bit superfluous as it is background
info rather than describing results.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. We agree that some portions of the
first Results section may read more like background. To address this, we have revised
the section to focus more explicitly on the experimental design process and the key
findings that guided the development. Background information has been moved to the
Introduction to maintain a clear distinction between context and results.
6. Are the fusion proteins in Fig 2e and Fig S4, referred to as SNAP-TMP-NLS and
H2B-SNAP-TMP-NLS the same? It appears so from the text but the nomenclature is
different.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The correct construct used in
both Figure 2e and Figure S8 is SNAP-TMP-NLS. The designation H2B-SNAP-TMP-
NLS was a labeling error in the text and has now been corrected to maintain consistency
throughout the manuscript and SI (line 77 and 139).
7. Line 227 – ‘MaP555-TMP show nice fluorogenicity (Fig. 2g and 2h)’ – is it not quite
weak?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and thoughtful comment.
MaP555-TMP exhibits a 13.3-fold increase in fluorescence intensity and achieves
approximately a 36.5-fold signal-to-noise ratio in live-cell imaging. Even at an elevated
probe concentration of 1 µM, only minimal nonspecific signal was detected. While its
fluorogenicity is somewhat lower compared to MaP618m-TMP (190-fold) and
MaP655-TMP (179-fold), MaP555-TMP still demonstrates reasonably robust
fluorogenic performance. To clarify this point and facilitate comparison with
MaP618m-TMP and MaP655-TMP, we have revised the manuscript to describe the
fluorogenicity as "moderate" rather than "nice". (line 226).
8. Fig 4, S23 – indicate the time between frames in the legend (and in other figures
showing time frames)
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and helpful suggestion. We
have now updated the figure legends to clearly indicate the time interval between
frames, using appropriate units (min, h, or s). Additionally, image frame numbers are
now marked with a "#" symbol for clarity.
9. Fig 4e – point out more clearly where the evidence of fission and fusion is (e.g.
highlighted regions as in Fig 5d).
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. In the revised version of
Fig. 4e, we have highlighted the regions where fission and fusion events occur in Fig.
5d and S28.
10. Fig. S26 – is it not supposed to also show the Hoechst staining in the Vimentin
labelled cells?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. In the revised version of
Fig. S26, we have repeated the confocal imaging to include Hoechst staining in the
vimentin-labeled cells. The updated data have been incorporated into the revised
Supplementary Information (Fig. S32).
11. Line 431 – ‘ReTag1 displayed only transiently reversible labeling, limiting its utility
for long-term tracking due to signal loss (Fig. 6i)’. How is this finding reconciled with
the analysis of ReTag1 in Fig. 3, which describes how it allows reversible labeling
within seconds to minutes in live-cell imaging, and fluorescence recovery within 1-2
minutes in the FRAP experiments? Perhaps this relates to the timing of the 400 frames,
but again I couldn’t find information about this in the legend or methods.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The distinction the
reviewer highlights arises from the differing contexts and timescales of the experiments.
In the FRAP experiments, the recovery of bulk H2B-ReTag1 fluorescence occurs within
1-2 minutes, representing ensemble-level dynamics in a high-density context. This
recovery reflects the exchange of many labeled proteins and may also be influenced by
factors such as protein localization, local environment, and probe concentration. By
contrast, in single-molecule tracking (Fig. 6i), individual fluorophores bound to ReTag1
are typically visible for only tens of frames at 20 Hz (approximately 1-2 seconds), after
which the signal is lost due to dissociation or photobleaching. This transient labeling
shown in Fig. 6i limits the continuous observation time of single molecules. To
overcome this limitation, we implemented multimeric constructs (e.g., ReTag4 or
ReTag8), which enable multi-fluorophore labeling and dynamic exchange. These arrays
help maintain signal despite fluorophore loss, thus extending the duration of single-
molecule tracking. We have clarified this distinction between ensemble fluorescence
recovery (FRAP) and single-molecule dwell time in the revised discussion and figure
legends (Lines 455).
12. Fig. 6i – explain how the number of fluorophores on individual proteins was
calculated.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To determine
the number of fluorophores bound to individual proteins in Fig. 6i, we performed
single-molecule brightness analysis using purified ReTag1 and ReTag4 constructs
immobilized on glass. Imaging was conducted under identical conditions (30% 640 nm
laser power, 30.4 W/cm²; 200 ms exposure). After background subtraction, the
fluorescence intensity of individual spots exhibited discrete levels corresponding to
integer multiples of a baseline intensity.
We first calibrated the signal using ReTag1, which binds exactly one MaP655-TMP
molecule. The fluorescence plateau intensity for ReTag1 was ~40 arbitrary units (a.u.),
which we define as the brightness of a single fluorophore. Since rhodamine dyes scale
linearly with copy number below saturation, we estimated fluorophore stoichiometry
by dividing the pre-bleach plateau intensity of each trace by 40 a.u. and rounding to the
nearest integer.
For ReTag4 labeled with 100 nM probe, the plateau intensities were typically ~80–
100 a.u., indicating ~2 bound fluorophores per protein. At 500 nM probe, the intensities
reached ~150–160 a.u., consistent with full occupancy of all four TMP-binding sites.
These discrete intensity levels and stepwise bleaching events further validated our copy
number estimation. This explanation has now been included in the revised Image data
analysis section (Lines 1200) for clarity.
13. Line 435 – ‘Even when one fluorophore was bleached or exchanged, other
fluorophores on ReTag4 continued to fluoresce, enabling extended single molecule
tracking to ~200 frames in a streaming acquisition (Fig. 6j)’. It looks like 100 frames
for reliable tracking for 100 frames, so better to say this or tracking up to 200 frames.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have revised the manuscript
to state "tracking over 100 frames" as suggested.
14. How does ReTag8 perform relative to ReTag4 in terms of fluorescence intensity and
brightness?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive
suggestion. Under 60% 640 nm laser intensity (99.1 W/cm2) with 50 ms exposure time,
we measured the single-molecule brightness of ReTag8-CAAX and ReTag4-CAAX.
The results show that ReTag8-CAAX is, on average, 1.5 times brighter than ReTag4-
CAAX. The data has been added in Fig. S38 of revised supplementary file.
15. Fig. 6k-o – representative images of cells used for the analysis should also be shown.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. In the revised manuscript,
we have added representative images of the cells used for the analysis in Fig. S37.
Point-By-Point Response to the Comments on the Manuscript “A Bright
and Regenerative Array Tag with Fluorogenic Ligands for Long-Term
Live-Cell Nanoscopy and Single-Molecule Tracking”
We are grateful to the reviewers for their insightful comments and
suggestions. In the revised manuscript we have attempted to address all
these points and changed the manuscript accordingly. Below we provide
a point-by-point response to the comments of the reviewers.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
1. The authors mentioned that the maximum FWHM of STED super-resolution
imaging is 43± 5 nm, and the laser energy used is 219 mW. However, the
authors also mentioned that the maximum laser energy of STED can reach 520
mW. According to STED imaging theory, the higher the STED light energy, the
higher the resolution. Why is the maximum resolution of this probe only 43 nm,
and not higher?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. In principle,
STED resolution improves with increasing depletion laser power. However, in
biological imaging the achievable resolution is constrained by several factors,
including imperfect overlap of excitation and depletion beams, residual intensity
at the central zero of the STED doughnut, detector signal-to-noise limitations,
and biological factors such as motion blur and sample heterogeneity. These
collectively prevent unlimited resolution gains in live-cell contexts [e.g., FWHM
of vimentin filaments reported as 39–52 nm (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2016, 55,
3290), 93–102 nm (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 3075), and 37 ± 4 nm (Nat.
Commun. 2022, 13, 2264)].
Regarding laser power, the maximum 520 mW value refers to the Leica SP8
STED system, whereas the STEDYCON system used in our study provides a
maximum depletion power of 370 mW. Under our conditions, we observed a
FWHM of ~43 ± 5 nm at 219 mW. Upon increasing the depletion power to 350
mW, the resolution improved modestly to ~40 ± 7 nm in living cells (new data
in Supplementary Fig. S27c). This value is close to the practical resolution limit
of the STEDYCON system (~30 nm in fixed samples under ideal conditions).
These new results and clarifications have been added to the revised
Supplementary Information.
2. If 219 mW laser energy is directly applied to the sample, it will directly cause
carbonization of the sample, not to mention the living cell experiment. The
author should provide the measurement position of the 219 mW laser energy
and also provide the laser energy directly acting on the sample.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue.
As requested, we calculated the actual laser power at the sample surface using
the STEDYCON system specifications:
𝑷 = 𝑷 ×𝜂 ×𝜂 ×𝜂
{𝒔𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆} {𝒍𝒂𝒔𝒆𝒓} {𝑠𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑚} {𝑝𝑎𝑡ℎ} {𝑜𝑏𝑒𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒}
Where P = 1.98 W (laser output power), η =59.137% (measured
laser system
modulation ratio of the laser system), η =25% (measured transmission
path
efficiency from laser exit to the objective entrance), η =75% (transmission
objective
efficiency of the objective lens). Substituting these values gives: P =1.98
sample
W×0.59137×0.25×0.75 ≈ 219 mW.
We fully agree with the reviewer that continuous irradiation with such high
powers could indeed damage biological samples. However, it is important to
note that STEDYCON employs pulsed STED excitation rather than
continuous-wave depletion (https://abberior.rocks/superresolution-confocal-
systems/stedycon/). Pulsed STED delivers depletion photons only within the
effective time window following excitation, thereby enhancing resolution while
minimizing photodamage. This pulsed approach also ensures tight temporal
synchronization between excitation and depletion pulses, maximizing depletion
efficiency while minimizing unnecessary light exposure (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.
U.S.A. 2000, 97, 8206–8210).
Indeed, STEDYCON has been widely applied in live-cell imaging without
observable sample carbonization (Angew Chem Int Ed Engl. 2022, 36,
e202207905; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2016, 55, 3290–3294). Consistent with
these reports, in our experiments we did not observe any carbonization or
irreversible photodamage in live-cell samples.
3. The STED and SIM imaging of mitochondria using FS27 and FS34 in the
article show that the probes target the outer mitochondrial membrane rather
than the inner membrane, and SIM imaging is better than STED. However,
STED imaging has a higher resolution than SIM. Why does this problem occur?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. While STED
microscopy inherently provides superior spatial resolution (as reflected by
narrower full width at half maximum, FWHM, values compared to SIM),
in our initial submission the SIM images appeared visually clearer than the STED
images. This apparent discrepancy stems from differences in image processing:
SIM data undergo computational reconstruction, including contrast
enhancement and noise reduction (using the HVL1 constrained deconvolution
algorithm or DFCAN/DFGAN deep learning algorithms, as described in the
Methods), whereas the STED images were presented as raw data without post-
processing.
To clarify this point, we have now (i) supplemented Fig. S27 with quantitative
FWHM analyses confirming the superior resolution of STED over SIM, and (ii)
applied deconvolution to the STED data to improve visual clarity. These
updates allow for a more balanced comparison between SIM and STED and
are explicitly noted in the revised figure legends and Methods section.
4. The authors mention that this probe has great advantages among STED
super-resolution imaging probes. However, according to the literature that has
been reported (Nature Communication 2020.11:3699, Proc. Natl Acad. Sci.
USA 116, 15817–15822 (2019). Biomedical Optics Express. 2024, 15(3):1595-
1604), the highest resolution of STED super-resolution imaging probes can
reach 35 nm and the longest imaging time can reach 60 minutes. Compared
with these probes, the probe mentioned by the authors does not have much
advantage in the field of STED super-resolution imaging. It can only be said
that this probe can be used for STED imaging, but it does not have a leading
advantage.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. We fully
agree that several excellent mitochondria-targeting dyes have been developed
for long-term STED imaging. For example, TPERh demonstrates high
photostability and low saturation power for cristae visualization (Biomed. Opt.
Express 2024, 15, 1595), while MitoESq-635 achieves ~35 nm resolution
and >50 min imaging of cristae dynamics in live cells (Nat. Commun. 2020, 11,
3699). These probes, similar to our reversible-binding approach, enable signal
recovery and prolonged imaging performance. However, their utility is largely
confined to mitochondria, particularly cristae structures, and cannot be

regenerative labeling and nanoscopy of diverse targets. Our ReTagX system

Live-Cell Nanoscopy and Single-Molecule Tracking”
We are grateful to the reviewers for their insightful comments and
suggestions. In the revised manuscript we have attempted to address all
these points and changed the manuscript accordingly. Below we provide
a point-by-point response to the comments of the reviewers.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
1. The authors mentioned that the maximum FWHM of STED super-resolution
imaging is 43± 5 nm, and the laser energy used is 219 mW. However, the
authors also mentioned that the maximum laser energy of STED can reach 520
mW. According to STED imaging theory, the higher the STED light energy, the
higher the resolution. Why is the maximum resolution of this probe only 43 nm,
and not higher?

STED resolution improves with increasing depletion laser power. However, in
biological imaging the achievable resolution is constrained by several factors,
including imperfect overlap of excitation and depletion beams, residual intensity
at the central zero of the STED doughnut, detector signal-to-noise limitations,
and biological factors such as motion blur and sample heterogeneity. These
collectively prevent unlimited resolution gains in live-cell contexts [e.g., FWHM
of vimentin filaments reported as 39–52 nm (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2016, 55,
3290), 93–102 nm (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 3075), and 37 ± 4 nm (Nat.
Commun. 2022, 13, 2264)].
Regarding laser power, the maximum 520 mW value refers to the Leica SP8
STED system, whereas the STEDYCON system used in our study provides a
maximum depletion power of 370 mW. Under our conditions, we observed a
FWHM of ~43 ± 5 nm at 219 mW. Upon increasing the depletion power to 350
mW, the resolution improved modestly to ~40 ± 7 nm in living cells (new data
in Supplementary Fig. S27c). This value is close to the practical resolution limit
of the STEDYCON system (~30 nm in fixed samples under ideal conditions).
These new results and clarifications have been added to the revised
Supplementary Information.
2. If 219 mW laser energy is directly applied to the sample, it will directly cause
carbonization of the sample, not to mention the living cell experiment. The
author should provide the measurement position of the 219 mW laser energy
and also provide the laser energy directly acting on the sample.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out this important issue.
As requested, we calculated the actual laser power at the sample surface using
the STEDYCON system specifications:
𝑷 = 𝑷 ×𝜂 ×𝜂 ×𝜂
{𝒔𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆} {𝒍𝒂𝒔𝒆𝒓} {𝑠𝑦𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑚} {𝑝𝑎𝑡ℎ} {𝑜𝑏𝑒𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒}
Where P = 1.98 W (laser output power), η =59.137% (measured
laser system
modulation ratio of the laser system), η =25% (measured transmission
path
efficiency from laser exit to the objective entrance), η =75% (transmission
objective
efficiency of the objective lens). Substituting these values gives: P =1.98
sample
W×0.59137×0.25×0.75 ≈ 219 mW.
We fully agree with the reviewer that continuous irradiation with such high

note that STEDYCON employs pulsed STED excitation rather than
continuous-wave depletion (https://abberior.rocks/superresolution-confocal-
systems/stedycon/). Pulsed STED delivers depletion photons only within the
effective time window following excitation, thereby enhancing resolution while
minimizing photodamage. This pulsed approach also ensures tight temporal
synchronization between excitation and depletion pulses, maximizing depletion
efficiency while minimizing unnecessary light exposure (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.
U.S.A. 2000, 97, 8206–8210).
Indeed, STEDYCON has been widely applied in live-cell imaging without

e202207905; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2016, 55, 3290–3294). Consistent with
these reports, in our experiments we did not observe any carbonization or
irreversible photodamage in live-cell samples.
